c.tagline: Gleaming desert metropolis on the Gulf.

emergency.note: 999 covers police, ambulance and fire; English-speaking operators are standard.

hood_landmark.West Bay: the glittering skyscraper skyline along the Corniche
hood_landmark.Msheireb: Msheireb Museums set in restored heritage courtyard houses
hood_landmark.Al Sadd: Jassim bin Hamad Stadium, home of Al Sadd SC
hood_landmark.Katara: Katara Cultural Village's hillside amphitheatre and golden mosque

avoid.reason: Crime is very low; the main cautions are aggressive driving when crossing roads and respecting local decency and photography rules rather than any specific area.

hood_desc: West Bay is Dohas gleaming high-rise business and diplomatic district packed with skyscrapers, luxury hotels and corporate offices, best for business travelers and those wanting a modern waterfront base near the Corniche.

The Pearl-Qatar is an upscale artificial island of Mediterranean-style marinas, designer boutiques and waterfront dining, ideal for luxury seekers and couples wanting a polished resort-like atmosphere.

Msheireb is a walkable, sustainably designed downtown regeneration district blending heritage museums with sleek modern architecture, suited to culture lovers and travelers wanting a central, pedestrian-friendly stay.
Al Sadd is a busy, authentic central residential and commercial area with shopping, local eateries and sports venues, good for budget-conscious travelers wanting an everyday Qatari city experience.
Katara is a cultural village of galleries, theaters, mosques and a public beach with a Mediterranean feel, perfect for arts enthusiasts and families seeking festivals and beachfront leisure.

water.note: Treated to international standards, though many opt for bottled water due to rooftop storage tanks.

transit.pay: Buy a rechargeable Travel (Karwa) card at any station ticket machine or customer-service desk, then tap in/out; single Standard-class trips run about QAR 2 (~$0.55), with day and weekly passes available, and Gold Club class costs more. Contactless bank-card tap-in is still limited, so getting a card first is easiest.
transit.hours: Metro runs Saturday-Wednesday roughly 6am-midnight, Thursday until 1am, and Friday afternoon-midnight only; check the app for exact daily times.

food.name: Machboos
food.desc: Qatar's national dish: rice cooked in spiced stock with chicken, lamb or hammour, dried lime and loomi, finished with a tangy daqoos sauce.

places.name: Shay Al Shomous
places.note: Started by Shams Al Qassabi, the souq's first Qatari businesswoman; the classic address.

places.name: Al Jasra Restaurant
places.note: Long-standing Qatari kitchen in the souq lanes, generous rice platters for sharing.

food.name: Harees
food.desc: Wheat and meat pounded for hours into a smooth, comforting porridge, topped with ghee; the Ramadan and wedding dish of the Gulf.

places.name: Al Tawash
places.note: Specialist Qatari kitchen; one of the easiest places to find harees outside Ramadan.

places.name: Souq Waqif home-cook stalls
places.note: Local women cook harees, madrouba and regag to order in the souq's food lanes.

food.name: Balaleet
food.desc: Sweet saffron vermicelli under a savoury omelette, the Qatari breakfast plate that turns sugar and eggs into one dish.

places.name: Shay Al Shomous
places.note: Widely called the best Qatari breakfast in Doha; go before 10am to get a table.

places.name: Karak Mqanes
places.note: Karak house that also does balaleet and regag; a proper local morning combination.

food.name: Thareed and madrouba
food.desc: Thareed layers spiced meat and vegetable stew over torn regag bread; madrouba is its creamy mashed-rice cousin.

places.name: Al Manchab Restaurant
places.note: Authentic Qatari menu built around stews, thareed and slow-cooked meats.

places.name: Souq Waqif home-cook stalls
places.note: Cheapest and most authentic thareed in the city, eaten at communal benches.

food.name: Khubz regag
food.desc: Paper-thin crepe cooked on a domed griddle and folded around cheese, egg, honey or Chips Oman, the Gulf's favourite crisp sandwich.

places.name: Souq Waqif regag stalls
places.note: Made in front of you on the hot plate; the cheese and Chips Oman version is a rite of passage.

places.name: Chapati and Karak
places.note: Cult breakfast stop for chapati, regag and karak; expect a queue at weekends.

food.name: Luqaimat
food.desc: Golf-ball dumplings fried crisp and drenched in date syrup or honey with sesame seeds, eaten hot in paper cones.

places.name: Souq Waqif sweet stalls
places.note: Fried to order in the evenings; the best value sweet in Doha.

places.name: Al Aker Sweets
places.note: Also famous for kunafa and baklava; good stop after dinner in the souq.

food.name: Karak chai
food.desc: Doha's national habit: black tea boiled with condensed milk, cardamom and saffron, sold from hatch windows for a couple of riyals.

places.name: Chapati and Karak
places.note: Ginger karak and warm sweet chapati; the most talked-about karak in Qatar.

places.name: Karak Mqanes
places.note: Strong, sweet, traditional Qatari style; pair it with regag or balaleet.

food.name: Gahwa
food.desc: Light-roast Arabic coffee with cardamom and saffron, poured from a dallah into small handleless cups and always served with dates.

places.name: Shay Al Shomous
places.note: Gahwa and dates served the way Qatari households do it, alongside breakfast.

places.name: Msheireb Downtown Doha cafes
places.note: Modern Qatari cafes pour gahwa with local dates in air-conditioned calm.

landmarks: Museum of Islamic Art (MIA)
I.M. Pei's striking geometric limestone building sits on its own island and houses a world-class collection, making its silhouette against the bay one of Doha's most photographed views.
Doha Corniche
This sweeping waterfront promenade offers postcard views of the West Bay skyline across the bay and is the city's favorite spot for sunset strolls and photos.
Souq Waqif
A restored traditional market with narrow lanes, spice stalls, falconry shops, and mud-rendered architecture, capturing old Qatari life in the heart of modern Doha.
Katara Cultural Village
A cultural district combining an amphitheater, mosques, galleries and a public beach, known for its striking Islamic-inspired architecture and public art installations.
West Bay Skyline
Doha's futuristic cluster of skyscrapers is best admired at night when illuminated, forming one of the most dramatic modern skylines in the Gulf.
The Pearl-Qatar
This man-made island of Mediterranean-style marinas, luxury towers, and waterfront promenades is a popular spot for upscale strolling and photography.
National Museum of Qatar
Designed by Jean Nouvel to resemble a desert rose crystal formation, this museum's swirling disc architecture is among the most distinctive in the world.
Msheireb Downtown Doha
A meticulously planned heritage-inspired downtown district blending traditional Qatari architecture with sustainable modern design and open plazas.
Aspire Tower (Torch Doha)
This distinctive torch-shaped tower, built for the 2006 Asian Games, is a defining feature of the Doha skyline, especially when lit at night.
Katara Towers
Two striking crescent-shaped hotel towers resembling traditional Qatari swords have become one of Doha's newest architectural icons on the West Bay Lagoon.

train.note: Qatar has no intercity passenger railway - the Doha Metro and Lusail Tram are urban only. Long-distance travel within Qatar and to neighbours is by road. A wider GCC rail network has long been planned but is not running in 2026.

intl.to: Dammam & Riyadh (Saudi Arabia) - via the Abu Samra/Salwa border
intl.op: SAPTCO and private transfer companies — tickets and visa checks arranged locally, no confirmed online booking

bus.note: There is no clean scheduled public international coach to confirm for 2026. Qatar's only land border is at Abu Samra (Salwa), leading to Saudi Arabia; SAPTCO and private transfer companies run Doha-Dammam and Doha-Riyadh road services, but confirm operator, times and visa rules before travelling. Mowasalat (Karwa) runs the domestic bus network within Qatar.

ferry.note: No scheduled international passenger ferries operate from Doha. Boats in the harbour are tourist dhow cruises only. To reach Saudi Arabia or Bahrain by land, cross by road via the Abu Samra/Salwa border.

half.name: Khor Al Adaid (Inland Sea)
half.blurb: A UNESCO-recognized inland sea where towering dunes meet the Gulf, reached by desert safari.

half.name: Al Zubarah Fort
half.blurb: UNESCO-listed 18th-century pearling town with a restored fort and vast archaeological ruins.

half.name: Zekreet & Ras Abrouq
half.blurb: Wind-carved mushroom rock formations and desert flats hosting Richard Serra's monumental steel sculpture.

half.name: Purple Island (Al Khor)
half.blurb: Peaceful mangrove islands rich with birdlife, best explored on foot or by kayak.

half.name: Al Jassasiya Rock Carvings
half.blurb: Qatar's largest rock-art site, with hundreds of ancient petroglyphs of boats and patterns.

half.name: Al Jumail Fishing Village
half.blurb: Hauntingly abandoned coastal settlement of crumbling stone homes and a lone mosque minaret.
